```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# Every chunk on this page runs from the folder of the case, so that the paths
# read exactly as they do in the workspace and in the browser lab:
# data/housing_audit.csv.
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = "../cases/housing")
```

```{r}
#| label: page-numbers
#| include: false
# The numbers quoted in the prose, computed from the curve of the case.
page_curve <- readr::read_csv("data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
ref_row    <- page_curve |> datawizard::data_filter(is_reference)
ref_gap    <- insight::format_value(ref_row$b_pp, digits = 2, style_negative = "minus")
```

This page introduces the helper functions with which the exercise of the housing-audit case fits its specifications, and the self-study route reads it in [stage 2](../tracks/self-study/stage-2.qmd). It assumes the R taught in [Getting started with R](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/r.html), the module on the umbrella site of the course, written on the data of this case, up to [section 10](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/r.html#sec-shares), in which the share of replies that greeted the sender by name is computed for two groups of names and the difference between the two shares is taken.

The code on this page ran when the page was built, and what R printed appears under each block, so you can compare your own output with the page line by line. Type each block into the workspace that you downloaded from the [setup page](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/setup.html#the-workspace), or into the [browser lab](../cases/housing/lab.qmd), where the helpers are already loaded.

## A first look at `try_spec()` {#sec-try-spec}

The workspace holds a file of helper functions, `R/spec_tools.R`, which the exercise loads once and then uses to fit specifications. A **specification** is one complete set of choices for an analysis: which names are compared, which emails are counted, what happens to the uncoded replies, which model is fitted and which covariates it holds. `source()` runs the file, so that its functions become available in your session. In the browser lab the helpers are already loaded, and the line is not needed.

```{r}
#| label: source-tools
#| eval: false
source("R/spec_tools.R")
```

```{r}
#| label: source-tools-page
#| include: false
# The page reads the helpers from the copy of the workspace beside the site,
# the nested repository in _workspaces/housing/, and its data/ from the folder
# of the case, which holds the same files.
source("../../_workspaces/housing/R/spec_tools.R")
```

`try_spec()` fits one specification and prints its result. Every argument has a default, and the defaults make up the reference specification, the comparison that section 10 of Getting started with R makes by hand, so calling the function with no arguments reproduces the gap computed there:

```{r}
#| label: try-reference
try_spec()
```

The first lines repeat the two shares and their difference, `r ref_gap` points, now with a 95% interval around it. The test line comes from a linear probability model, a regression of the 0/1 outcome on an indicator of the Hispanic names, whose coefficient is exactly the difference in shares; the [binary-outcomes module](binary-outcomes.qmd) explains it. The last lines give the number of replies analysed, a partial correlation computed by the rule of the Multi100 project, the class of the result, and its place among the `r nrow(page_curve)` specifications of the curve of the claim.

Changing one argument changes one decision. `population = "all"` counts every delivered email, as the second calculation of that section does:

```{r}
#| label: try-all
try_spec(population = "all")
```

Options that are not on the curve are refused, with the reason why and the page of the course site that teaches them. Here the outcome is set to any reply rather than a greeting by name, which would answer a different claim:

```{r}
#| label: try-refused
#| error: true
try_spec(outcome = "reply")
```

Every call to `try_spec()` is logged, and `my_experiments()` prints the log, showing only the decisions that you varied:

```{r}
#| label: my-experiments
my_experiments()
```

That is the whole of Task 4 in miniature: change one decision at a time, read what moves, and keep a record. The [exercise overview](../cases/housing/exercise.qmd) sets out the five tasks, the [specification menu](../cases/housing/menu.qmd) lists every argument and its options, and the [cheatsheet](../cases/housing/cheatsheet.qmd) puts the helpers on one page.
